items.literal_translation: Much pleasure.
items.usage_note: Standard reply when introduced to someone; works in any setting. The other person often answers 'Igualmente' (likewise).

items.literal_translation: How does it go to you?
items.usage_note: Casual greeting with friends or peers (tú). With someone you address as usted, say '¿Cómo le va?'.

items.literal_translation: From where are you?
items.usage_note: Informal tú form for peers. Answer with 'Soy de...' plus a place.

items.literal_translation: From where are you (formal)?
items.usage_note: Formal version for older people, officials or strangers. Usted takes third-person verb forms: 'es', not 'eres'.

items.literal_translation: With permission.
items.usage_note: Said when passing in front of someone or leaving a group. To get attention or apologize, use 'Disculpe' or 'Perdón' instead.

items.literal_translation: Excuse (me), where is the bathroom?
items.idiomatic_translation: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
items.usage_note: 'Disculpe' is the usted command form, polite with strangers and staff. 'Estar' is used for location: 'dónde está'.

items.literal_translation: Me can (you) help, please?
items.usage_note: Polite usted request. The object pronoun 'me' can also attach to the infinitive: '¿Puede ayudarme?'.

items.literal_translation: I don't understand. Can (you) repeat it more slowly?
items.idiomatic_translation: I don't understand. Could you say that again more slowly?
items.usage_note: Essential learner phrase. 'Lo' (it) attaches to the end of the infinitive 'repetir'.

items.literal_translation: How much does (it) cost?
items.usage_note: Asking a price. For several items use the plural: '¿Cuánto cuestan?'.

items.literal_translation: The bill, please.
items.usage_note: In most of Latin America the server will not bring the bill until you ask for it.

items.literal_translation: What hour is it?
items.usage_note: Answer with 'Es la una' for one o'clock and 'Son las...' for every other hour.

items.literal_translation: I have hunger.
items.usage_note: Spanish uses 'tener' (to have) for many physical states: tengo sed (thirsty), tengo frío (cold), tengo sueño (sleepy).

items.literal_translation: I have to go myself.
items.usage_note: 'Tener que' plus an infinitive expresses obligation. 'Irse' (to leave) is reflexive, so the 'me' attaches to it.

items.literal_translation: We see each other tomorrow.
items.usage_note: Friendly goodbye; drop 'mañana' for a general 'see you'. 'Nos' here means 'each other'.

items.literal_translation: I feel it a lot.
items.usage_note: A sincere apology or condolence. For a minor bump or interruption, 'Perdón' is lighter.

items.literal_translation: It makes much heat today.
items.usage_note: Weather often uses 'hacer': hace frío (it's cold), hace sol (it's sunny), hace viento (it's windy).

items.literal_translation: Can I pay with card?
items.usage_note: Useful before ordering in small shops, where some places accept only cash ('efectivo').

items.literal_translation: This song enchants me.
items.usage_note: 'Encantar' works like 'gustar': the thing loved is the subject. For plural things: 'Me encantan estas canciones'.

items.literal_translation: I am of agreement.
items.usage_note: Use 'estar', not 'ser'. To disagree politely: 'No estoy de acuerdo'.

items.literal_translation: It gives me equal.
items.usage_note: Neutral way to say you have no preference. Tone matters: said flatly, it can sound like 'I don't care'.

items.literal_translation: You all already ate?
items.usage_note: In Latin America 'ustedes' is the only plural 'you', for friends and strangers alike, and takes third-person plural verbs ('comieron').

items.literal_translation: That it may go well for you.
items.usage_note: Warm farewell using the subjunctive 'vaya'. Formal: 'Que le vaya bien'; to a group: 'Que les vaya bien'.

items.phrase: ¿Me podría traer un vaso de agua?
items.literal_translation: Could (you) bring me a glass of water?
items.idiomatic_translation: Could you bring me a glass of water?
items.usage_note: The conditional 'podría' softens a request and is very polite with servers and staff.

items.literal_translation: Do you lend me your charger?
items.usage_note: Spanish asks the other person to lend ('prestar') rather than saying 'can I borrow'. Informal tú form; formal: '¿Me presta su cargador?'.

items.literal_translation: It forgot itself on me.
items.usage_note: This 'accidental se' frames forgetting as something that happened to you. The more direct 'Olvidé...' is also correct.

items.literal_translation: To what do you dedicate yourself?
items.idiomatic_translation: What do you do for a living?
items.usage_note: Common, polite way to ask about someone's job. Formal: '¿A qué se dedica?'.

items.literal_translation: Right-now-ish I come.
items.usage_note: Very common in Mexico. 'Ahorita' can mean 'right away' or 'in a while', so context and tone decide how soon.

items.literal_translation: I'm going to take the truck.
items.idiomatic_translation: I'm going to take the bus.
items.usage_note: In Mexico 'camión' means a city bus. Other countries say 'bus', 'autobús' or 'colectivo'; 'ir a' plus an infinitive expresses the near future.

items.literal_translation: What wave?
items.usage_note: Casual greeting among friends, especially in Mexico and Central America. Avoid with strangers or in formal settings.

items.literal_translation: How father!
items.usage_note: Mexican slang for enthusiasm. Elsewhere in Latin America 'genial' or '¡qué bueno!' is more widely understood.

items.literal_translation: There is nothing of what.
items.usage_note: Common reply to 'gracias'. 'De nada' is equally standard; 'No hay de qué' sounds slightly warmer.

items.literal_translation: I need to go to the doctor.
items.idiomatic_translation: I need to see a doctor.
items.usage_note: 'a' + 'el' contracts to 'al'. 'Médico' and 'doctor' are both used for a physician.

items.literal_translation: The head hurts me.
items.usage_note: 'Doler' works like 'gustar': the body part is the subject. Spanish uses 'la' (the), not 'mi', for body parts here.

items.literal_translation: At what hour do (they) open?
items.usage_note: 'Abren' is third-person plural: it addresses the staff as ustedes or refers to 'they'. Ask '¿A qué hora cierran?' for closing time.

items.phrase: Quisiera hacer una reservación para dos personas.
items.literal_translation: I would like to make a reservation for two people.
items.idiomatic_translation: I'd like to book a table for two.
items.usage_note: 'Quisiera' is a polite softened 'I want'. Latin America says 'reservación'; Spain usually says 'reserva'.

items.literal_translation: Is the tip included?
items.usage_note: Worth asking: some restaurants add a service charge, while in others a tip of about 10% is expected.

items.literal_translation: What do you (formal) recommend me?
items.usage_note: Polite way to ask a server or shop assistant for advice. Informal: '¿Qué me recomiendas?'.

items.literal_translation: Where does the metro station remain?
items.usage_note: In Latin America 'quedar' is very common for the location of places; '¿Dónde está...?' also works.

items.phrase: Siga derecho y luego dé vuelta a la izquierda.
items.literal_translation: Continue straight and then give turn to the left.
items.usage_note: Directions use usted commands ('siga', 'dé'). 'Dar vuelta' is common in Latin America; 'girar' and 'doblar' are also understood.

items.literal_translation: How much time does one take to arrive?
items.idiomatic_translation: How long does it take to get there?
items.usage_note: Impersonal 'se' makes it general ('does one take'). For yourself: '¿Cuánto tiempo tardo en llegar?'.

items.literal_translation: Don't worry yourself.
items.usage_note: Negative informal command uses the subjunctive. Formal: 'No se preocupe'; to a group: 'No se preocupen'.

items.literal_translation: Good benefit!
items.usage_note: Said to people who are eating, even strangers at a nearby table when you pass or leave. Reply: 'Gracias, igualmente'.

items.literal_translation: I finish of arriving.
items.usage_note: 'Acabar de' plus an infinitive means 'to have just done' something.

items.literal_translation: I am looking for work.
items.usage_note: Present progressive (estar + -ando/-iendo) for an ongoing action. 'Buscar' already includes 'for': no preposition needed.

items.phrase: Tengo ganas de ir a la playa.
items.literal_translation: I have desires of going to the beach.
items.idiomatic_translation: I feel like going to the beach.
items.usage_note: 'Tener ganas de' plus an infinitive expresses wanting to do something right now.

items.literal_translation: It was without wanting.
items.idiomatic_translation: It was an accident. / I didn't mean to.
items.usage_note: Standard way to say an action was unintentional, often after bumping someone or breaking something.

items.literal_translation: Could (you all) speak more slowly, please?
items.idiomatic_translation: Could you all speak more slowly, please?
items.usage_note: Polite request to a group, using the ustedes conditional 'podrían'.

items.literal_translation: It already made itself late on me.
items.usage_note: Very common across Latin America, especially Mexico. The 'se me' construction frames lateness as something that happened to you.

items.literal_translation: Your brother falls well to me.
items.usage_note: 'Caer bien' means you like someone as a person, without romantic overtones. 'Me cae mal' means you dislike them.

items.phrase: Hace dos años que estudio español.
items.literal_translation: It makes two years that I study Spanish.
items.idiomatic_translation: I've been studying Spanish for two years.
items.usage_note: 'Hace' + time + 'que' + present tense describes an action that started in the past and continues now.

items.literal_translation: It is worth the pain.
items.usage_note: Often followed by an infinitive: 'Vale la pena visitar el museo'. Negative: 'No vale la pena'.

items.literal_translation: May God will that it does not rain tomorrow.
items.idiomatic_translation: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
items.usage_note: 'Ojalá' comes from Arabic and always takes the subjunctive ('llueva'). The 'que' is optional.

items.literal_translation: It took me by surprise.
items.usage_note: Preterite of 'tomar'. In Spain 'me pilló por sorpresa' is also common; 'tomar' is the safe pan-Latin-American choice.

items.literal_translation: I thank you all much your help.
items.idiomatic_translation: Thank you all very much for your help.
items.usage_note: 'Les' addresses ustedes as the indirect object. More formal and emphatic than 'gracias'; good for emails and speeches.

items.literal_translation: Can you wrap it for me for gift?
items.idiomatic_translation: Could you gift-wrap it for me?
items.usage_note: Two object pronouns: indirect 'me' comes before direct 'lo'. Many shops wrap purchases for free when asked.

items.literal_translation: Does it beat for you?
items.usage_note: Mexican slang for checking if someone likes a plan. Answer 'Me late' (I'm in). Avoid outside casual settings.

items.literal_translation: Throw desire at it.
items.idiomatic_translation: Give it your all. / You've got this.
items.usage_note: Common Mexican encouragement before an exam, game or hard task. To a group: 'Échenle ganas'.

items.literal_translation: More is worth late than never.
items.usage_note: Proverb used the same way as in English, often jokingly to someone who arrives late.

items.phrase: Si tuviera más tiempo, viajaría más.
items.literal_translation: If I had more time, I would travel more.
items.idiomatic_translation: If I had more time, I'd travel more.
items.usage_note: Hypothetical: 'si' + imperfect subjunctive ('tuviera'), then the conditional ('viajaría'). Never use the conditional after 'si'.

items.literal_translation: Can you recommend me a good restaurant?
items.idiomatic_translation: Can you recommend a good restaurant?
items.usage_note: Informal tú request to a friend or peer. 'Bueno' shortens to 'buen' before a masculine singular noun.

items.literal_translation: What such your end of week?
items.usage_note: A standard Monday greeting at work or school. 'Qué tal' works for any 'how was' question.

items.literal_translation: I raise myself early between week.
items.idiomatic_translation: I get up early on weekdays.
items.usage_note: 'Entre semana' means Monday to Friday; the opposite is 'el fin de semana'.

items.literal_translation: Would it please you to go to the cinema with me?
items.idiomatic_translation: Would you like to go to the movies with me?
items.usage_note: A polite invitation. 'Gustar' works backwards: the outing pleases you.

items.phrase: Está a dos cuadras de aquí.
items.literal_translation: It is at two blocks from here.
items.usage_note: 'Cuadra' is the usual Latin American word for a city block; Spain says 'manzana'.

items.phrase: ¿A qué hora sale el próximo autobús?
items.literal_translation: At what hour leaves the next bus?
items.idiomatic_translation: What time does the next bus leave?
items.usage_note: 'Autobús' is understood everywhere; in Mexico city buses are also called 'camión'.

items.literal_translation: Pardon, I mistook myself of number.
items.usage_note: 'Equivocarse de' + noun means to pick the wrong one: 'me equivoqué de calle' is 'I took the wrong street'.

items.literal_translation: Can you charge me, please?
items.idiomatic_translation: Can I pay, please? / Could you ring me up?
items.usage_note: Used at a counter or to a waiter in Mexico when you want to pay.

items.phrase: Quiero cambiar esta camisa por una talla más grande.
items.literal_translation: I want to change this shirt for a size more big.
items.idiomatic_translation: I'd like to exchange this shirt for a bigger size.
items.usage_note: 'Cambiar X por Y' means to exchange X for Y. Use 'talla' for clothes and 'número' for shoes.

items.literal_translation: Do you have something more cheap?
items.usage_note: Uses 'usted' (tiene) with a shop assistant; with a friend say '¿tienes...?'.

items.literal_translation: I stayed asleep.
items.usage_note: Also means 'I fell asleep'. A woman says 'me quedé dormida'.

items.literal_translation: I carry half hour waiting.
items.idiomatic_translation: I've been waiting for half an hour.
items.usage_note: 'Llevar' + time + gerund expresses how long something has been going on.

items.literal_translation: Do you pass me the salt?
items.idiomatic_translation: Can you pass me the salt?
items.usage_note: Requests at the table use the present tense; it sounds natural, not rude.

items.literal_translation: To me it finished the battery.
items.usage_note: The 'se me' construction presents accidents as things that happened to you.

items.literal_translation: Where can I take a taxi?
items.idiomatic_translation: Where can I get a taxi?
items.usage_note: 'Tomar' is the normal Latin American verb for catching transport.

items.literal_translation: I am colded.
items.usage_note: A woman says 'estoy resfriada'. In Mexico 'tengo gripa' is at least as common for a cold.

items.literal_translation: Can I leave a message?
items.usage_note: Useful on the phone or at a reception desk.

items.literal_translation: It goes to rain more late.
items.usage_note: 'Ir a' + infinitive is the everyday way to talk about the near future.

items.literal_translation: Which is your favourite food?
items.usage_note: With 'ser' + noun, Spanish asks '¿cuál?' where English says 'what'.

items.phrase: Me falta un poco de práctica.
items.literal_translation: To me lacks a little of practice.
items.idiomatic_translation: I need a bit more practice.
items.usage_note: 'Faltar' works like 'gustar': the thing that is missing is the subject.

items.literal_translation: Already you finished?
items.usage_note: 'Ya' in a question means 'yet' or 'already'. Latin America prefers the simple past here.

items.literal_translation: Pass to it, you are in your house.
items.idiomatic_translation: Come on in, make yourself at home.
items.usage_note: A warm Mexican welcome at the door. 'Pásale' also invites customers into a shop.

items.literal_translation: Is there a pharmacy near?
items.usage_note: 'Hay' means 'there is/are' and never changes for plural.

items.literal_translation: It doesn't stay well on me.
items.usage_note: 'Quedar' describes how clothes fit or suit you: 'te queda muy bien' means 'it looks great on you'.

items.literal_translation: We stay at the eight.
items.usage_note: 'Quedar' also means to arrange to meet. 'Quedamos en el café' sets the place.

items.literal_translation: Do you notify me when you arrive?
items.idiomatic_translation: Will you let me know when you get there?
items.usage_note: 'Cuando' about the future takes the subjunctive: 'llegues', not 'llegas'.

items.literal_translation: I have hurry.
items.usage_note: In Mexico 'tengo prisa' and 'ando con prisa' are both common.

items.literal_translation: What do I put on myself?
items.usage_note: 'Ponerse' means to put on clothes; 'ponte un suéter' means 'put on a sweater'.

items.literal_translation: I fell myself from the bicycle.
items.usage_note: 'Caerse' takes the reflexive pronoun when you fall.

items.literal_translation: Can you lower to it at the volume?
items.idiomatic_translation: Can you turn the volume down?
items.usage_note: 'Bajarle' and 'subirle' are everyday Mexican for turning sound down or up.

items.literal_translation: Already almost I arrive.
items.usage_note: A standard reply to '¿dónde estás?'. The present tense describes the near future.

items.literal_translation: To me it would have pleased to go.
items.idiomatic_translation: I would have liked to go.
items.usage_note: The past subjunctive 'hubiera' expresses regret about something that did not happen.

items.literal_translation: It is not for so much.
items.idiomatic_translation: It's not that big a deal.
items.usage_note: Used to calm someone down or to downplay a problem.

items.literal_translation: It gives me shame to ask it of him.
items.usage_note: In Mexico 'pena' usually means embarrassment; in other countries it often means sorrow.

items.literal_translation: At the best I arrive late.
items.usage_note: 'A lo mejor' means 'maybe' and takes the indicative, unlike 'quizás', which often takes the subjunctive.

items.literal_translation: More worth to prevent than to lament.
items.usage_note: A common saying when you take a precaution.

items.literal_translation: I tell it to you in seriousness.
items.usage_note: Stresses that you are not joking.

items.literal_translation: Not a way.
items.idiomatic_translation: Oh well. / Nothing we can do.
items.usage_note: Very common in Mexico to accept a setback calmly.

items.literal_translation: I am up to the cap.
items.usage_note: Mexican and Central American. 'Estoy harto' is the general equivalent.

items.phrase: Se me hace que va a llover.
items.literal_translation: To me it makes itself that it goes to rain.
items.idiomatic_translation: I think it's going to rain.
items.usage_note: In Mexico 'se me hace que' introduces a hunch or impression.

items.literal_translation: At the while I dial you.
items.idiomatic_translation: I'll call you in a bit.
items.usage_note: Mexican: 'al rato' means 'later on', and 'marcar' means to phone someone.

items.literal_translation: When you have time, you notify me.
items.idiomatic_translation: Let me know when you have time.
items.usage_note: 'Cuando' referring to the future takes the subjunctive 'tengas'.

items.literal_translation: Although it may rain, we go to go.
items.idiomatic_translation: Even if it rains, we're going.
items.usage_note: 'Aunque' + subjunctive means 'even if'; with the indicative it means 'even though'.

items.literal_translation: It cost me a lot to accustom myself.
items.idiomatic_translation: It took me a long time to get used to it.
items.usage_note: 'Costar' expresses difficulty as well as price: 'me cuesta levantarme temprano'.

items.literal_translation: I don't have not even idea.
items.usage_note: The double negative is correct and emphatic in Spanish.

items.literal_translation: That depends on you.
items.usage_note: Spanish uses 'depender de', with 'de' where English uses 'on'.

items.literal_translation: Does it matter to you if I open the window?
items.idiomatic_translation: Do you mind if I open the window?
items.usage_note: A polite request for permission; with 'usted' say '¿le importa...?'.

items.literal_translation: I am at point of leaving.
items.usage_note: 'Estar a punto de' + infinitive means 'to be about to'.

items.literal_translation: Now to it! (from 'ahora' + 'le')
items.idiomatic_translation: Come on! / Wow! / OK, let's do it!
items.usage_note: A very Mexican word whose meaning depends on tone: encouragement, surprise or agreement.

items.literal_translation: It costs me work to concentrate myself.
items.idiomatic_translation: I find it hard to concentrate.
items.usage_note: 'Costar trabajo' is the usual Mexican way to say something is hard for you.

items.literal_translation: I did it on purpose.
items.usage_note: 'A propósito' also means 'by the way' at the start of a sentence.

items.literal_translation: Without wanting, wanting.
items.usage_note: Made famous by the Mexican TV character El Chavo del Ocho; used jokingly.

items.phrase: Hay que ver el lado positivo.
items.literal_translation: There is to see the positive side.
items.idiomatic_translation: You have to look on the bright side.
items.usage_note: 'Hay que' + infinitive gives a general obligation, with no specific subject.

items.literal_translation: Already the twenty fell to me.
items.usage_note: Mexican: from old pay phones, where the call connected once the 20-centavo coin dropped.

items.literal_translation: He threw me the blame.
items.usage_note: 'Echarle la culpa a alguien' is the everyday way to say 'to blame someone'.

items.literal_translation: This is in Chinese.
items.idiomatic_translation: This is really hard to understand.
items.usage_note: Mexican expression for something very difficult, like 'it's all Greek to me'.

items.literal_translation: To me it urges to speak with you.
items.idiomatic_translation: I really need to talk to you.
items.usage_note: 'Me urge' is common in Mexico for anything urgent: 'me urge un café'.

items.literal_translation: I entrust it to you.
items.idiomatic_translation: I'm counting on you with this. / Please take care of it.
items.usage_note: In Mexico also a friendly way to ask a favour: 'te encargo las llaves'.

items.literal_translation: Let's throw it an eye.
items.idiomatic_translation: Let's take a look at it.
items.usage_note: 'Echar un ojo' or 'echar un vistazo' means to have a quick look.

items.literal_translation: Hopefully I had studied more.
items.idiomatic_translation: I wish I had studied more.
items.usage_note: 'Ojalá' + past perfect subjunctive expresses regret about the past.

items.literal_translation: If I could, I would help you.
items.idiomatic_translation: If I could, I'd help you.
items.usage_note: A hypothetical: imperfect subjunctive in the 'si' clause, conditional in the result.
